Students often claim that they study better while listening to music, chatting online and checking notifications. Psychologists, however, point out that the brain does not truly do several tasks at once; it switches rapidly between them, and each switch costs a little time and attention. A student who answers a message in the middle of a chemistry problem may need several minutes to regain the same depth of focus. Over an evening, these small losses add up to a serious waste. In one classroom experiment, two groups were given the same reading task. The group that worked without interruptions finished earlier and answered more questions correctly. Yet the members of the second group were convinced that they had worked well. This false confidence is, perhaps, the most worrying finding. It suggests that the problem is not only distraction but also our poor judgement of how distracted we are.

In a drought-prone block of Rajasthan, the administration repaired old stepwells instead of laying a costly pipeline from a distant river. Critics called the decision backward-looking. They argued that a pipeline was modern, visible and politically impressive, while stepwells belonged to the past. The officer in charge, Ms Rathore, replied that the pipeline would take six years to complete and would depend on a river that was itself shrinking. The stepwells, on the other hand, could be restored within a season, were cheaper to maintain and were already known to the villagers, who understood when and how they filled. Two monsoons later, the repaired stepwells held water through the summer for the first time in thirty years. Ms Rathore does not claim that pipelines have no place in planning. Her point is narrower: a solution should be judged by whether it fits local conditions and can be delivered in time, not by how modern it appears.
